'''Helsby''' is a village, [[Civil parishes in England|civil parish]] and [[Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom|electoral ward]] in the unitary authority of [[Cheshire West and Chester]] and the ceremonial county of [[Cheshire]], England. Overlooking the [[River Mersey|Mersey estuary]], it is approximately {{convert|9|mi|km|0}} north east of [[Chester]] and {{convert|2.5|mi|km|0}} south west of [[Frodsham]].

In the [[2001 United Kingdom census|2001 census]] the civil parish of Helsby had a population of 4,701.<ref>{{NOMIS2001|id=13UH020|title=Helsby Parish|access-date=21 February 2021}}</ref>  By the [[United Kingdom Census 2011|2011 census]] this had risen to 4,972.<ref>{{NOMIS2011|id=E04011112|title=Helsby Parish|access-date=21 February 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ukcensusdata.com/helsby-e05008678#sthash.Qvv94g32.dpbs|title=Ward/community population 2011|access-date=28 May 2015|archive-date=5 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305163514/http://www.ukcensusdata.com/helsby-e05008678#sthash.Qvv94g32.dpbs|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Geography==
[[File:Helsby Hill view - geograph.org.uk - 5978405.jpg|thumb|Outlook from atop Helsby Hill]]
The village is situated on the [[A56 road|A56 main road]] between [[Chester]] and [[Runcorn]]. The neighbouring settlements are [[Dunham Hill, Cheshire|Dunham-on-the-Hill]], [[Frodsham]], [[Elton, Cheshire|Elton]] and [[Alvanley]]. Helsby is a semi-rural village, with a few [[Dairy farming|dairy]] and [[Arable land|arable]] farms, but is also in close proximity to a number of industrial plants around the [[River Mersey|Mersey estuary]] including the [[Essar Energy|Essar]] [[Stanlow Oil Refinery]], the Encirc glass bottle manufacturing plant, the Kemira [[fertiliser]] plant on [[Ince, Cheshire|Ince]] Marshes and the Ineos Chlor chemical manufacturing site and power station at [[Rocksavage]]. There are few jobs in Helsby itself. The [[Tesco]] supermarket is one of the biggest employers in Helsby. The village is popular with [[Commuting|commuters]] as a residential area, due to its links to the [[M56 motorway]] and rail networks.

==History==
On Helsby Hill, the remains of a promontory hillfort, 1.9ha in area, have been excavated. A buried soil was found under the hillfort containing fossilised pollen dating to the late Mesolithic to early Neolithic, between 7000 and 3001 BC.<ref>http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH8237 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904131431/http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH8237 |date=4 September 2014}} Revealing Cheshire's Past HER number 1007/2</ref> Further evidence suggests a burning episode dating to the early Neolithic occupation or woodland clearance dating to 4000BC to 2351 BC.<ref>http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH22371 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904131600/http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH22371 |date=4 September 2014}} Revealing Cheshire's Past HER number 1007/1</ref>

The bivallate hillfort is protected on the south and east by two parallel ramparts and an unusual type of inturned entrance 11 yards (10 m) wide. There were three phases of hillfort construction at Helsby. The first stone rampart was constructed in the middle to late Bronze Age (1250–1050 cal BC) and consisted of a bank with a well-dressed outer face of sandstone blocks and an irregular inner face, which was built on a slight batter; it was approximately 4 yards (3.5m) wide. A socketed bronze axe was found at Helsby in 1925.<ref>http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH8042{{dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot}} Revealing Cheshire's Past HER number 1004</ref> This was followed by a series of colluvial deposits against the internal face of the stone rampart that formed the second phase of activity. The third and final phase was the re-building of the rampart in the post-Roman period, dating as late as 530 AD suggesting early Saxon re-occupation of the hillfort.<ref>http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH8237 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904131431/http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH8237 |date=4 September 2014}} Reveal Cheshire's Past HER number 1007/2</ref>

Helsby was located on the strategically important [[Roman road]] between Chester and [[Wilderspool]] near [[Warrington]]. The road existed between c. 79–410 AD to link the garrison of Deva to Wilderspool, which produced pottery that supplied the north west of England.<ref>http://potsherd.net/atlas/Ware/WPMO Potsherd – Atlas of Roman Pottery</ref> The Roman road passed at the foot of Helsby Hill probably following the route of Old Chester Road.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cheshirewestandchester.gov.uk/microsites/habitats_and_hillforts/about/idoc.ashx?docid=2e2843b5-4d36-4742-9230-e06babce4ecf&version=-1 |title=Archived copy |access-date=2014-08-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140903074209/http://www.cheshirewestandchester.gov.uk/microsites/habitats_and_hillforts/about/idoc.ashx?docid=2e2843b5-4d36-4742-9230-e06babce4ecf&version=-1 |archive-date=3 September 2014 |df=dmy-all}} Helsby Hill and Woodhouse Hillfort 2010</ref> On the top of the hill a Roman bronze sestertius of the emperor Tiberius minted in Rome in AD22 was found and just off Vicarage Lane in 1958, an uninscribed Roman altar of red sandstone was discovered with a carved jug on one side and an axe and knife on the other.<ref>http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH7695 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904131422/http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH7695 |date=4 September 2014}} Revealing Cheshire's Past HER number 1008</ref>

The first known settlers of Helsby were the [[Vikings]] in the 10th century{{Citation needed|date=November 2009}}. In fact, the name 'Helsby' is likely to be derived from the Viking name ''Hjallr-by'', meaning "the village on the edge" (placenames with the [[suffix]] ''"by"'' often denote Viking/Danish origins, e.g. Derby, Grimsby, Whitby, etc.). However, Old Norse suggests that Hjalli means edge and Hjallr means constructed platform or scaffold.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nordicnames.de/wiki/Hjalli |title=Hjalli|publisher=Nordic names|access-date=30 August 2014}}</ref>

The village was recorded in the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086 under the [[Normans|Norman]] name of ''Hellesbe''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.domesdaybook.co.uk/cheshire1.html |title=Cheshire A-K: Helsby|publisher=Domesday Book Online|access-date=4 February 2009}}</ref> The Manor of Helsby was owned by a series of [[Aristocracy (class)|aristocratic]] landowners, most recently the [[Marquess of Cholmondeley]].

In the 13th century Helsby was deemed a demesne manor under the lordship of Dunham-on-the-Hill, by a family called Hellesby. Later it passed to Thornton and then to Frodsham. The earliest mention of the original, timber Old Hall, was in a contract for the construction of additional work in stone in the mid 15th century. The wooden part of the hall perished in a fire in the 16th century when it was leased to one of the Hatons of Helsby. The later hall probably derived its name from its proximity to the older site. It was built of brick at the end of the 18th century and was used as a farmhouse.<ref>http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH7697 {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140904131649/http://rcplive.cheshire.gov.uk/SingleResult.aspx?uid=MCH7697 |date=4 September 2014}} Revealing Cheshire's Past HER number 1012/1</ref>

Helsby Hill was the location of a rare public execution when William Henry Clarke was hung in chains on 21 April 1791 after being convicted of robbing the Warrington Mail.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britishexecutions.co.uk/execution-content.php?key=9920 |title=William Henry Clarke|publisher=British Executions|access-date=30 August 2014}}</ref>

==Community==
[[File:St Paul's, Helsby (1).JPG|thumb|[[St Paul's Church, Helsby|St Paul's Anglican Church]]]]
A Methodist church was established in 1800, seventy years before the [[Anglican]] church was built in 1870. Helsby is home to two primary schools (Helsby Hillside and Hornsmill) that serve the east and west of the village respectively, with the former being in close proximity to one of the most successful secondary schools in Cheshire for the 2018/2019 academic year: [[Helsby High School]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.compare-school-performance.service.gov.uk/schools-by-type?step=phase&region=896&geographic=la&phase=16to18 |title=All schools and colleges in Cheshire West and Chester|website=Find and compare schools in England|publisher=GOV.UK|language=en|access-date=21 February 2021}}</ref>

The village was once home to many [[Public house|pubs]], the majority of which were adjacent to the [[A56 road]]. 

A community Christmas event, Ho Ho Helsby, was held for the second time on 2 December 2017, with an estimated attendance of 2,500 people. It features artisan stalls, ice skating, reindeer, live music from local musicians and a twilight procession of floats featuring local schools, community groups and businesses. Knitted angels are hidden around the village in the run up to Christmas Day. The village also has its own craft beer, Ho Ho Helsbeer, brewed in a brewery less than two miles away. The event is organised entirely by volunteers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.helsbyparishcouncil.gov.uk/our-community/ho-ho-helsby/ |title=Ho Ho Helsby |publisher=Helsby Parish Council |access-date=8 May 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://hohohelsby.co.uk/ |title=Home page |publisher=Ho Ho Helsby |access-date=8 May 2025}}</ref>

==Transport==
[[File:Helsby Railway Station - geograph.org.uk - 6004308.jpg|thumb|Helsby Railway Station]]
The railway came to Helsby in 1850, with the construction of the line between Chester and [[Warrington]]. [[Helsby railway station]] has won awards as one of the best kept unmanned stations in the UK. The [[signal box]] at Helsby Junction is still operated manually. Services are operated at approximately hourly intervals by [[Transport for Wales Rail|Transport for Wales]] to [[Manchester Piccadilly railway station|Manchester Piccadilly]] and in the other direction to [[Chester railway station|Chester]] and [[North Wales|Llandudno]]. There is also a regular Transport For Wales service connecting Helsby from Chester to [[Liverpool Lime Street railway station|Liverpool Lime Street]] during the day and early evening as of 2024. The village had another railway station, [[Helsby and Alvanley railway station]], which is closed.

There is also a minimal ([[Parliamentary train|parliamentary]]) service operated by [[Northern (train operating company)|Northern]] to neighbouring [[Ince and Elton railway station|Ince & Elton]] and [[Stanlow and Thornton railway station|Stanlow & Thornton]] with trains terminating at [[Ellesmere Port railway station|Ellesmere Port]] where a connection is made with the [[Merseyrail]] electric service to Liverpool.

There are frequent bus links: X30 (Warrington to Chester), and X2 (Runcorn to Ellesmere Port). All these run Monday to Saturday only.

==Industry and economy==
The factory site at the western end of the village has been for many years the main source of employment in the village. Originally built in 1884 by the Telegraph Manufacturing Company as the Britannia Telegraph Works, it manufactured telegraph and telephone cables. Early advertisements for cable hands specified that he "must be a good cricketer"! The company was taken over by the [[Automatic Telephone Manufacturing Company]] and the telephone equipment and instrument  manufacturing sections moved to [[Liverpool]] in 1892.<ref>{{Cite book | last =  Robertson | first = J. H. | year = 1947 | title = The Story of the Telephone: A History of the Telecommunications Industry of Britain | publisher = Pitman | location = London | isbn =  |pages=96–98 }}</ref> The cable works was more recently owned by [[British Insulated Callender's Cables|BICC]] to make electronic cables. At peak employing 5,000 people, the number of workers declined from the Second World War. The decline continued following a series of [[redundancy (law)|redundancy]] initiatives started in 1970, and the site eventually closed in 2002. The site was then redeveloped for retail, light industrial and residential purposes. The first completed development on the site was a [[Tesco]] supermarket, which opened in September 2005.  In 2005 cable manufacturing returned to Helsby when Heat Trace Limited, a British specialist cable manufacturer, took over one of the last remaining industrial buildings on the site to expand their operations, taking advantage of the existence of the electron beaming unit on the site for the irradiation of their specialist heating cables.

North west of Helsby, near the village of [[Ince, Cheshire|Ince]], landowners [[The Peel Group]] are developing a {{convert|54|ha|acre}} [[Ince Park|industrial site on marshland]]. In 2009 a public inquiry gave permission to build a [[biomass]] power station,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/merseyside/8196878.stm |title=Waste power plant plan approved|publisher=BBC News|date=12 August 2009|access-date=12 August 2009}}</ref> which opened in 2018<ref>{{Cite web|title=First 'waste' energy generated at Protos in Cheshire|url=https://www.letsrecycle.com/news/latest-news/energy-generated-protos-cheshire/ |date=2 May 2018|access-date=5 February 2021|website=letsrecycle.com|language=en}}</ref>  as part of the Protos "energy and resource hub".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.protos.co.uk/destination/ |title=Protos: Destination|publisher=Peel L&P|access-date=21 December 2020}}</ref>  The site also houses a timber recycling plant and designated "nature areas".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.protos.co.uk/site-availability/ |title=Protos: Site availability|publisher=Peel L&P|access-date=21 December 2020}}</ref>   
The construction of a facility to recover energy from non-recyclable waste began in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.letsrecycle.com/news/latest-news/biffa-reaches-financial-close-on-protos-efw/ |title=Biffa, Covanta & GIG in financial close on Protos EfW|website=letsrecycle.com|date=1 December 2020|access-date=21 December 2020}}</ref>

==Landmarks==
===Helsby Hill===
[[File:Helsby, The Hill in the Snow - geograph.org.uk - 208875.jpg|thumb|Helsby Hill]]
The village sits at the foot of a wooded [[sandstone]] hill {{convert|463|ft}} [[above sea level]]. Helsby Hill has steep cliffs on the northern and western sides and is a prominent landmark rising above the [[Cheshire Plain]] and overlooking the [[River Mersey|Mersey estuary]]. Much of the hill is owned and managed by the [[National Trust]]. It is the site of [[Helsby hill fort]], an ancient British [[hillfort]], and more recently acquired a concrete pillar [[trig point]] on its summit. The top of the hill also has a former [[Royal Observer Corps]] post, which was abandoned in 1992.{{Citation needed|date=November 2008}} Visitors who see Helsby Hill from the M56 or on the train can sometimes see a man's face within the cliff face from east, west and sometimes from the north. This is referred to as the "Old Man of Helsby".

;Access to hill
Numerous footpaths, running from the public roads encircling the hill, give ready access for walkers. One such path, known as Hill Road, runs through a large sandstone cutting, which was the route of a railway in the Second World War. The hilltop offers views of the Welsh hills and, on exceptionally clear days, [[Snowdon]]. The landmarks of [[Liverpool]] can clearly be seen beyond the Helsby marshes, [[Stanlow Oil Refinery]], the [[Kemira]] [[fertiliser]] plant and the [[Manchester Ship Canal]]. Also on very clear days, visitors can see across [[Lancashire]], past [[Bolton]], to [[Winter Hill (North West England)|Winter Hill]] with its  [[Winter Hill transmitting station|TV Mast]]. The view looking back is not as diverse, but the [[Peckforton Hills]] and [[Beeston Castle]] can be discerned.

;Rock climbing
The craggy face of the hill provides many routes for rock climbers at a range of grades from easy climbs suitable for beginners (some of which do not require ropes), to challenging climbs up to a grade 6c. The cliff is also split into two lateral sections. The main face is easily accessible from the ground. At the top is a large grassy area, followed by an easily accessible 10-foot (or thereabouts) cliff to the summit, which is excellent for [[bouldering]]. Despite its often slimy appearance, the cliff's sandstone composition means it dries out quickly after rain, and, after several accidents, several large metal spikes were placed at the top of the main cliff for top-rope climbing that offer extra safety for climbers worried about the sandstone's crumbly nature.{{Citation needed|date=April 2010}} Two quarries in [[Harmers Wood]], southwest of Helsby Hill, feature over sixty climbs of varying difficulty.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ukclimbing.com/logbook/crag.php?id=12388|title=Harmer's Wood|website=Ukclimbing.com|accessdate=10 January 2019}}</ref>

===Mountskill Quarry===
[[File:The Tunnel, Mountskill Quarry - geograph.org.uk - 175825.jpg|thumb|Mountskill Quarry]]
[[Sandstone]] was extracted from a working quarry from the early 19th century until the 1920s. Much of the stone was transported by ferry to [[Liverpool]] and [[Birkenhead]], where several buildings, including the Customs House near [[Canning Dock]], were built of Helsby stone. The quarry originally had its own dedicated horse-drawn tramway link to [[Ince, Cheshire|Ince]] Pier. After stone production ceased, it was not until the late 1980s that an alternative use was found for the site and in the intervening decades the derelict site was used as a tip by local residents. The site was acquired by the former [[Vale Royal Borough Council]] in 1988 and transformed into a woodland park, which was opened in 1990. 'Helsby Quarry Woodland Park' is now managed by [[Cheshire West and Chester]] Council. It contains a range of trees including [[oak]], [[Acer pseudoplatanus|sycamore]], [[rowan]], [[Betula pendula|silver birch]], [[willow]] and [[beech]]—some of which grew naturally during the site's period of dereliction, and some of which were planted specifically in preparing the woodland park.{{Citation needed|date=June 2009}} The [[woodland]] and [[grassland]] are inhabited by many animal and bird species.{{Citation needed|date=June 2009}} Aside from the [[wildlife]], the geology of the site is one of its most significant features and it is designated a [[Regionally Important Geological Site]]. The site features exposed rock walls and a tunnel, which enable sandstone formations from the [[Triassic]] period (251–199 million years ago) to be viewed.

2604773.extract:
Wicken Fen is a 254.5-hectare (629-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest west of Wicken in Cambridgeshire. It is also a National Nature Reserve, and a Nature Conservation Review site. It is protected by international designations as a Ramsar wetland site of international importance, and part of the Fenland Special Area of Conservation under the Habitats Directive.
A large part of it is owned and managed by the National Trust.
It is one of Britain's oldest nature reserves, and was the first reserve cared for by the National Trust, starting in 1899. The first parcel of land for the reserve was donated to the Trust by Charles Rothschild in 1901. The reserve includes fenland, farmland, marsh, and reedbeds. Wicken Fen is one of only four wild fens that still survive in the enormous Great Fen Basin area of East Anglia. There  99.9% of the former fens have been replaced by arable cultivation.

==Reserve==

===Management===
[[Image:Wicken Fen Windpump.jpg|left|upright|thumb|The windpump at Wicken Fen]]
Humans have managed Wicken Fen for centuries, and the reserve is still managed intensively to protect and maintain the delicate balance of species that has built up over the years.

Much of the management tries to recreate the old systems of fen working that persisted for hundreds of years, allowing species to become dependent on the practices. For example, the sedge plant, ''[[Cladium mariscus]]'', is harvested every year and sold for thatching roofs. The earliest recorded sedge [[harvest]] at Wicken was in 1414,<ref>Rowell, T.A. (1983). History and Management of Wicken Fen. PhD thesis, University of Cambridge.</ref> and ever since then, sedge has been regularly cut. The sedge-cutting has resulted in an array of animals, fungi, and plants colonizing the area that depend on regular clearance of the sedge in order to survive.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2008-12-16 |title=Fungi of Wicken Fen, Cambridgeshire: an annotated list |url=http://www-biol.paisley.ac.uk/research/Asilverside/wicken/Wicken_flist.html |access-date=2023-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081216031109/http://www-biol.paisley.ac.uk/research/Asilverside/wicken/Wicken_flist.html |archive-date=16 December 2008 }}</ref> (Many animals, plants and fungi are dependent upon such regular management of vegetation to keep their habitats intact.<ref name=":0" />) As part of the management plan for Wicken Fen, [[Konik|Koniks]] and [[Highland cattle]] have been introduced to some areas for grazing, in order to prevent scrub from regrowing, with additional scrub clearance carried out by rangers.

===Windpump===
Wicken Fen features the last surviving wooden [[windpump]] in the Fens. It is a small [[smock mill|smock]] wind pump, which was built by Hunt Brothers Millwrights, [[Soham]], in 1908 at nearby Adventurers' Fen {{see below}} for drainage of [[peat]] workings. It is an iron-framed structure with wooden [[weatherboarding]]. There are four {{convert|30|ft|0|adj=on}} sails driving a {{convert|13|ft|adj=on}} [[scoop wheel]]. The pump was moved to its present site and restored in 1956 by the National Trust. 

In a reversal of its original function, it now raises water from the drainage channel, through a height of {{convert|4|ft}}, to maintain the level in the reed beds.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Labrum |first1=E. A. |title=Civil engineering heritage. Eastern and central England |date=1994 |publisher=[[Institution of Civil Engineers]] |location=London |isbn=9780727719706 |page=107}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nationalmillsweekend.co.uk/pages_wind/wicken%20Fen.htm |title=National Mills Weekend: Wicken Fen mill |access-date=9 November 2015 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304055125/http://www.nationalmillsweekend.co.uk/pages_wind/wicken%20Fen.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Science===
[[File:British Swallowtail Wicken Fen.jpg|thumb|Specimen of Swallowtail butterfly, collected from Wicken Fen]]
The Fen has been long associated with natural history. [[Charles Darwin]] collected beetles on the site in the 1820s. Many eminent Victorian naturalists collected beetles, moths and butterflies at Wicken Fen; some of their collections can still be found in museums. Many nationally rare species have been recorded, including the [[Old world swallowtail|swallowtail]] butterfly until its decline and eventual loss from the fen in the 1950s, and despite an attempt to reintroduce it.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/botanists-pave-way-for-return-of-swallowtail-britains-largest-butterfly-is-to-grace-a-fen-where-1491529.html|title=Botanists pave way for return of swallowtail: Britain's largest butterfly is to grace a fen where ideal habitat has been created|date=14 June 1993|author=Peter Victor|work=The Independent}}</ref>
From the 1920s onwards the fathers of modern [[ecology]] and [[conservation biology|conservation]], the Cambridge [[botany|botanists]] Sir [[Arthur Tansley]] and Sir [[Harry Godwin]], carried out their pioneering work on the reserve. One of the world's longest-running science experiments, the [[Godwin Plots]], continues at the Fen to this day. The Fen's long association with science, especially nearby [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]], continues to the present day with scientists actively involved in the management of the reserve. Many hundreds of research papers have been published about the fen over more than a century. A Bibliography can be downloaded from the Wicken website and the latest Newsletter.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wicken.org.uk/research.htm|title=Research|publisher=Wicken Fen|access-date=5 November 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130528230606/http://www.wicken.org.uk/research.htm|archive-date=28 May 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Facilities===
The Fen is open to the public. The site is open all year round from dawn to dusk except for [[Christmas Day]]. Some paths are closed in very wet weather, and some areas are inaccessible. However, a boardwalk leading to two bird hides is open all of the time. There are several bird hides and many miles of trails for visitors to follow. 

There are also a visitor centre, shop, and [[café]]. The visitor centre has a permanent exhibition of information about Wicken Fen, its history and ecological importance. The Fen Cottage is open on most days, showing the life of fen people at the turn of the 20th century.<ref name=wicken/>

==Development of the reserve==
[[File:Wicken Fen NT map.svg|thumb|upright|National Trust land at Wicken Fen in 2011.<ref>[http://www.wicken.org.uk/maps/wickenmaps_walkers.pdf Maps of National Trust owned land at Wicken Fen] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111119173335/http://www.wicken.org.uk/maps/wickenmaps_walkers.pdf |date=19 November 2011 }}, Retrieved 18 December 2011</ref>]]
On 1 May 1899, the National Trust purchased two acres (8094 m<sup>2</sup>) for £10, and by 2016 the reserve site had more than 800 acres.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wicken.org.uk/history/|title=Wicken Fen: The History|publisher=National Trust|access-date=13 December 2016|archive-date=20 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220113259/http://www.wicken.org.uk/history/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The ecology of the Fen was studied in the first decade of the 1900s by [[Richard Henry Yapp]].<ref name="Yapp-Sketches">{{cite Q|Q101626317}}</ref>

===The Wicken Fen Vision===
The Wicken Fen Vision is a project of the National Trust; its plan over a 100-year period is to expand the protected fen area to a size of {{convert|56|km2|sqmi|abbr=on}}. It was launched in 1999 to mark the 100th anniversary of the first acquisition. In 2001 a major acquisition was made with the purchase of Burwell Fen Farm (1.65 km<sup>2</sup>). In 2005, a 100 ha turf farm, to be called Tubney Fen, was purchased. Other purchases include Hurdle Hall Farm and Oily Hall Farm in 2009, and St Edmunds Fen in 2011.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-trust/w-thecharity/w-annualreports.htm |title=National Trust Annual Reports |access-date=31 December 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111226185547/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-trust/w-thecharity/w-annualreports.htm |archive-date=26 December 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The National Trust aims to acquire further land as it becomes available, paying market prices.<ref name=WFV1>
{{cite web
|url=http://www.wicken.org.uk/vision.htm
|title=The Wicken Vision - Introduction
|publisher=[[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]
|access-date=2011-12-30
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120525075337/http://www.wicken.org.uk/vision.htm
|archive-date=25 May 2012
|url-status=dead
}}
</ref> As a result of the increased area of wetlands, the populations of skylarks, snipe, grey partridge, widgeon and teal have all increased, with a major increase in barn owls and short-eared owls. Buzzards, hen and marsh-harriers have returned, and bitterns began breeding here by 2009 for the first time since the 1930s.<ref>http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-access-annual-report-09.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629112744/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-access-annual-report-09.pdf |date=29 June 2011 }} National Trust Annual Report 2009)</ref>

The Wicken Fen Vision has great support from many people and organisations. Large sums of money have been raised from grant-awarding bodies, and from individual donors. Enlargement of the reserve has faced criticism from some residents of nearby settlements. An on-line petition entitled 'SaveOurFens' stated "We the undersigned petition the Prime Minister to Stop the National Trust flooding or junglefying our Cambridgeshire Fens!". Concerns centred on the issues of loss of agricultural land and increases in levels of local traffic and [[mosquito]] populations. A petition named '{{Not a typo|wickenfenvision}}', in favour of the scheme, was also held. The two petitions ended in 2010, with a two to one vote in favour of the Wicken Fen Vision.<ref>[http://www.hmg.gov.uk/epetition-responses/petition-view.aspx?epref=wickenfenvision Petition supporting the Vision] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111011140742/http://www.hmg.gov.uk/epetition-responses/petition-view.aspx?epref=wickenfenvision |date=11 October 2011 }}, 846 votes; [https://savethefens.blogspot.com/ Petition against the Vision], 418 votes</ref>

=== Lodes Way ===
[[File:Wicken fen spine route.png|thumb|Lodes Way sustainable transport route]]
As part of the Vision project, the National Trust, in conjunction with [[Sustrans]], opened a sustainable transport route connecting Wicken Fen with [[Anglesey Abbey]] and Bottisham. Work on the paths and bridges began in 2008 and was scheduled for completion in 2011.<ref>
{{cite web
|url=http://www.wicken.org.uk/vision_swaffhambridge.htm
|title=Vision Bridges the Gap
|publisher=National Trust
|date=2010-04-18
|access-date=2011-12-30
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718230206/http://www.wicken.org.uk/vision_swaffhambridge.htm
|archive-date=18 July 2011
|url-status=dead
}}
</ref> The new walking, cycle and horse riding route is {{convert|9|miles|km}} long, and includes a number of minor roads as well as new paths and bridges to link the gap in the existing Sustrans [[National Cycle Route 11]] between Cambridge and Ely. The project, originally called the Wicken Fen Spine Route, includes the construction of a series of new bridges over the man-made waterways known as [[Cambridgeshire Lodes|Lodes]]. In July 2008, the new Swaffham Bulbeck Lode bridge and a half-mile cycle and bridleway path across White Fen were opened. Upgrades to the crossing of the River Cam at Bottisham Lock and the bridge over Burwell Lode are planned. A new bridge over Reach Lode was opened in September 2010 and an upgraded cycle way across Burwell Fen is nearly complete.<ref name=WFV2>
{{cite web
|url=http://www.wicken.org.uk/vision_lodesway.htm
|title=The Wicken Vision - Lodes Way
|publisher=[[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]
|access-date=2011-12-30
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120113112200/http://www.wicken.org.uk/vision_lodesway.htm
|archive-date=13 January 2012
|url-status=dead
}}
</ref> The total cost of the scheme is £2 million, £600,000 of which are from [[Sustrans]]'s [[Connect2]] scheme.<ref name=C2>
{{cite web
|url=http://www.sustransconnect2.org.uk/news/news_detail.php?item=Cambridge+to+Wicken+Fen+walking+and+cycling+network+%96+now+a+step+closer+
|archive-url=https://archive.today/20121224213057/http://www.sustransconnect2.org.uk/news/news_detail.php?item=Cambridge+to+Wicken+Fen+walking+and+cycling+network+%96+now+a+step+closer+
|url-status=dead
|archive-date=2012-12-24
|title=Cambridge to Wicken Fen walking and cycling network – now a step closer
|publisher=[[Sustrans]]
|date=2009-03-04
|access-date=2009-07-14
}}
</ref>

===Habitats===
[[Image:Wicken Lode1.JPG|thumb|left|Wicken Lode]]
Wicken Fen is divided by a man-made watercourse called "[[Cambridgeshire Lodes|Wicken Lode]]". The area north of Wicken Lode, together with a smaller area known as Wicken Poors' Fen and St. Edmunds Fen, forms the classic old, undrained fen. The designated [[national nature reserve (United Kingdom)|national nature reserve]] of 269 hectares also includes the area around the Mere, to the south of Wicken Lode. These areas contain original [[peat]] fen with communities of [[carr (fen)|carr]] and [[Cyperaceae|sedge]]. They support rare and uncommon fenland plants such as marsh pea, Cambridge milk parsley, fen violet and marsh fern. This part of the Fen can be enjoyed from a series of boardwalks (made from recycled plastic).

The area south of the Lode is called "Adventurers' Fen" and consists of rough pasture (grading from dry to wet grassland), reedbed and pools.

The dykes, abandoned clay pits and other watercourses carry a great wealth of aquatic plants and insects, many of which are uncommon elsewhere.

==Biodiversity==
Naturalists were originally drawn to Wicken because of its species richness and the presence of rarities. The Fen has received a great deal of recording effort and as a result, huge species lists have accumulated. Surveys continue to the present day. In 1998 more than 20 species new to the Fen were recorded for the first time, and in 2005 another 10 were added.

Many of the species lists can be downloaded from the Fen website (see below). Wicken Fen was established as a nature reserve because of its [[invertebrate]] and plant interest. Over 10,000 species have so far been recorded on the fen,<ref>{{cite news |last1=Prickett |first1=Katy |title=Rare moth becomes Wicken Fen's 10,000th recorded species |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crl56w46ex1o |access-date=14 October 2025 |work=[[BBC News]] |date=8 October 2025}}</ref> including more than 125 that are included in the [[Red Data Book]] of rare invertebrates.<ref name=wildlife>{{cite web|url=http://www.wicken.org.uk/wildlife.htm|title=Wildlife|publisher=Wicken Fen|access-date=24 May 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229224751/http://www.wicken.org.uk/wildlife.htm|archive-date=29 December 2010|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Invertebrates===
The reserve supports large numbers of fly, snail, spider and beetle species. Damselflies found here include the [[Lestes sponsa|emerald]], [[Azure damselfly|azure]], [[Large red damselfly|large red]], [[red-eyed damselfly|red-eyed]], [[Variable damselfly|variable]] and [[Common blue damselfly|common blue]]; together with dragonflies such as the [[Southern hawker|southern]] and [[brown hawker]]s, [[Emperor (dragonfly)|emperor]], [[hairy dragonfly]] and [[black-tailed skimmer]]. The Lepidoptera fauna is very rich also, especially moths, with more than 1000 species including the nationally rare [[reed leopard]] and [[Marsh Carpet|marsh carpet]]. Other local moths include [[cream-bordered green pea]], [[yellow-legged clearwing]] and [[Pavonia pavonia|emperor]]. China-mark moths, such as the [[Cataclysta lemnata|small]], [[Elophila nymphaeata|brown]] and [[Parapoynx stratiotata|ringed]], are also seen here. Local butterflies include the [[green hairstreak]], [[brown argus]], [[Speckled wood (butterfly)|speckled wood]] and [[Brimstone (butterfly)|brimstone]]. There are a range of freshwater and land snails including the Red Data Book species [[Desmoulin's whorl snail]].<ref name=wildlife/>

===Birds===
[[Image:4566.reed warbler holding food.jpg|thumb|right|A [[Eurasian reed warbler]] at Wicken Fen]]
The site is mainly noted for its plants and invertebrates, but many birds also can be seen. These are particularly popular with visitors as they are often easier to observe than the more elusive insects and plants.

Bird species recorded living at the site include [[great crested grebe]], [[Great cormorant|cormorant]], [[gadwall]], [[Common teal|teal]], [[Eurasian sparrowhawk|sparrowhawk]], [[water rail]], [[European kingfisher|kingfisher]], [[Common snipe|snipe]], [[Eurasian woodcock|woodcock]], [[Great spotted woodpecker|great spotted]] and [[European green woodpecker|green woodpecker]]s; and [[Western barn owl|barn]], [[Little owl|little]], [[Tawny owl|tawny]], [[Long-eared owl|long-eared]] and [[short-eared owl]]s. Visiting birds include [[Great bittern|bittern]], [[whooper swan]], [[Eurasian golden plover|golden plover]], [[garganey]], [[Common pochard|pochard]], [[goosander]], [[marsh harrier]], [[hen harrier]], [[Merlin (bird)|merlin]] and [[Eurasian hobby|hobby]]. In season, it is most unlikely that visitors will fail to hear the 'drumming' of [[Common snipe|snipe]].<ref name=wildlife/>

=== Fungi ===
Recording of fungi at Wicken goes back at least to 1924, with a first checklist published in 1935.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Transactions of the British Mycological Society 19 (4): 280, 1935 |url=http://www.cybertruffle.org.uk/cyberliber/59351/0019/004/0280.htm |access-date=2023-09-25 |website=www.cybertruffle.org.uk}}</ref> There are now more than 700 species of fungi known from the reserve,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wicken Fen (NT) {{!}} Pan-species Listing |url=https://psl.brc.ac.uk/content/wicken-fen-nt |access-date=2023-09-25 |website=psl.brc.ac.uk}}</ref> representing at least 38 different orders.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |date=2008-12-16 |title=Fungi of Wicken Fen, Cambridgeshire: an annotated list |url=http://www-biol.paisley.ac.uk/research/Asilverside/wicken/Wicken_flist.html |access-date=2023-09-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081216031109/http://www-biol.paisley.ac.uk/research/Asilverside/wicken/Wicken_flist.html |archive-date=16 December 2008 }}</ref> About 130 of these species are [[lichen]]-forming, and about 120 others were found in soil.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Transactions of the British Mycological Society 36 (4): 304, 1953 |url=http://www.cybertruffle.org.uk/cyberliber/59351/0036/004/0304.htm |access-date=2023-09-25 |website=www.cybertruffle.org.uk}}</ref> Many of the others are [[Saprotrophic nutrition|saprobes]] on decaying plant material, including several species associated only with fenland plants. [[Ectomycorrhizal extramatrical mycelium|Ectomycorrhizal]] fungi, which typically prefer well-drained soils, are few: despite the presence of substantial oaks on fairly open, moderately dry ground in the reserve's carr thickets, oak-specific mycorrhizal toadstools are largely and perhaps wholly absent. The probable explanation is that those oaks are recent, and no more likely to be mycologically productive than any new and artificial plantation.<ref name=":1" />

===Plants===
Notable plants include the [[Viola persicifolia|fen violet]], [[Cladium mariscus|great fen sedge]], [[Lathyrus palustris|marsh pea]], [[Ranunculus lingua|greater spearwort]], [[marsh orchid]]s and [[Peucedanum palustre|milk parsley]]. There are also a number of [[Charales|stonewort]] species present in the ditches and ponds, along with [[Butomus umbellatus|flowering rush]], [[Myriophyllum verticillatum|water milfoil]], and yellow and white water lilies.

3103645.title: Little Moreton Hall
3103645.extract:
Little Moreton Hall, also known as Old Moreton Hall, is a moated half-timbered manor house 4.5 miles (7.2 km) south-west of Congleton in Cheshire, England. The earliest parts of the house were built for the prosperous Cheshire landowner William Moreton in about 1504–08 and the remainder was constructed in stages by successive generations of the family until about 1610. The building is highly irregular, with three asymmetrical ranges forming a small, rectangular cobbled courtyard. A National Trust guidebook describes Little Moreton Hall as being "lifted straight from a fairy story, a gingerbread house." The house's top-heavy appearance, "like a stranded Noah's Ark", is due to the Long Gallery that runs the length of the south range's upper floor.
The house remained in the possession of the Moreton family for almost 450 years, until ownership was transferred to the National Trust in 1938. Little Moreton Hall and its sandstone bridge across the moat are recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade I listed building; the ground on which Little Moreton Hall stands is protected as a Scheduled Monument. The house has been fully restored and is open to the public from April to December each year.
At its greatest extent, in the mid-16th century, the Little Moreton Hall estate occupied an area of 1,360 acres (550 ha); it contained a cornmill, orchards, gardens and an iron bloomery with water-powered hammers. The gardens lay abandoned until their 20th-century re-creation. As there were no surviving records of the layout of the original knot garden, it was replanted according to a pattern published in the 17th century.

'''Little Moreton Hall''', also known as '''Old Moreton Hall''',{{efn|The house was known as Old Moreton Hall during the period when it was rented out to tenant farmers, from the late 1670s onwards.{{r|Survival}}}} is a [[moat]]ed [[timber framing|half-timbered]] [[manor house]] {{nowrap|{{convert|4.5|mi|km}}}} south-west of [[Congleton]] in [[Cheshire]], England.{{r|HowToGetHere}} The earliest parts of the house were built for the prosperous Cheshire landowner William Moreton in about 1504–08 and the remainder was constructed in stages by successive generations of the family until about 1610. The building is highly irregular, with three asymmetrical ranges forming a small, rectangular [[cobblestone|cobble]]d courtyard. A [[National Trust]] guidebook describes Little Moreton Hall as being "lifted straight from a fairy story, a gingerbread house."{{sfnp|Fedden|Joekes|1984|p=19|ps=none}} The house's top-heavy appearance, "like a stranded [[Noah's Ark]]", is due to the Long Gallery that runs the length of the south range's upper floor.{{sfnp|Greeves|2006|p=226|ps=none}}

The house remained in the possession of the Moreton family for almost 450 years, until ownership was transferred to the National Trust in 1938. Little Moreton Hall and its sandstone bridge across the moat are recorded in the [[National Heritage List for England]] as a designated Grade I [[listed building]];{{r|Images}}{{r|NHLE}} the ground on which Little Moreton Hall stands is protected as a [[Scheduled Monument]].{{r|NHLE}}{{efn|Little Moreton Hall is built on the site of a much earlier medieval building; the remains of which are believed to have survived in the ground under the present house.{{r|NHLE}}}} The house has been fully restored and is open to the public from April to December each year.

At its greatest extent, in the mid-16th century, the Little Moreton Hall estate occupied an area of {{convert|1360|acre}}; it contained a [[gristmill|cornmill]], orchards, gardens and an iron [[bloomery]] with [[trip hammer|water-powered hammer]]s. The gardens lay abandoned until their 20th-century re-creation. As there were no surviving records of the layout of the original [[knot garden]], it was replanted according to a pattern published in the 17th century.

==History==
[[File:Great Hall, Little Moreton Hall.jpg|thumb|left|upright|The Great Hall, looking west towards the screens passage]]
The name Moreton probably derives from the [[Old English]] ''mor'' meaning "marshland" and ''ton'', meaning "town". The area where Little Moreton Hall stands today was named Little Moreton to distinguish it from the nearby township of [[Moreton cum Alcumlow]], or Greater Moreton. The Moreton family's roots in Little Moreton can be traced to the marriage in 1216 of Lettice de Moreton to Sir Gralam de Lostock, who inherited land there; succeeding generations of the de Lostocks adopted the name of de Moreton.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=28|ps=none}} Gralam de Lostock's grandson, Gralam de Moreton, acquired valuable land from his marriages to Alice de Lymme and then Margery de Kingsley. Another grandson, John de Moreton, married heiress Margaret de Macclesfield in 1329, adding further to the estate.{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|pp=177–78|ps=none}} The family also purchased land cheaply after the [[Black Death]] epidemic of 1348.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=2|ps=none}} Four generations after John de Moreton, the family owned sixteen [[messuage]]s, a mill and {{convert|700|acre}} of land, comprising 560 acres of ploughland, 80 acres of pasture, 20 acres of meadow, 20 acres of wood and 20 acres of [[bog|moss]].{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|pp=178–79|ps=none}} The [[dissolution of the monasteries]] in the mid-16th century provided further opportunities for the Moretons to add to their estate,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=2|ps=none}} and by the early years of [[Elizabeth I]]'s reign, William Moreton II owned two water mills and {{convert|1360|acre}} of land valued at £24 7s 4d, including 500 acres of ploughland, 500 acres of pasture and 100 acres of [[turbary]].{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|p=180|ps=none}}

Little Moreton Hall first appears in the historical record in 1271, but the present building dates from the early 16th century.{{r|NHLE}}{{efn|Many older sources, such as Pevsner & Hubbard (1971), suggest that building work began in c. 1450, or towards the end of the 15th century, but [[dendrochronology|tree-ring analysis]] shows that the earliest parts of the house were built in the first decade of the 16th century.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=28|ps=none}}{{sfnp|Hartwell|Hyde|Hubbard|Pevsner|2011|p=433|ps=none}}}} The north range is the earliest part of the house. Built between 1504 and 1508 for William Moreton (died 1526), it comprises the [[Great Hall]] and the northern part of the east wing.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=9–15|ps=none}} A service wing to the west, built at the same time but subsequently replaced, gave the early house an H-shaped floor plan.{{sfnp|Hartwell|Hyde|Hubbard|Pevsner|2011|p=433|ps=none}} The east range was extended to the south in about 1508 to provide additional living quarters, as well as housing the Chapel and the Withdrawing Room.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=9–15|ps=none}} In 1546 William Moreton's son, also called William (c. 1510–63), replaced the original west wing with a new range housing service rooms on the ground floor as well as a porch, gallery, and three interconnected rooms on the first floor, one of which had access to a [[garderobe]].{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=28|ps=none}} In 1559 William had a new floor inserted at gallery level in the Great Hall,{{efn|The floor had been removed by 1807.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=9|ps=none}}}} and added the two large bay windows looking onto the courtyard, built so close to each other that their roofs abut one another.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=9|ps=none}}{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The south wing was added in about 1560–62 by William Moreton II's son John (1541–98).{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=4|ps=none}} It includes the Gatehouse and a third storey containing a {{convert|68|ft|m|adj=on}} [[Long Gallery]],{{sfnp|Fedden|Joekes|1984|p=155|ps=none}} which appears to have been an afterthought added on after construction work had begun.{{sfnp|Greeves|2008|p=201|ps=none}} A small kitchen and Brew-house block was added to the south wing in about 1610, the last major extension to the house.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=29|ps=none}}

[[File:Elizabethan Fireplace, Little Moreton Hall.jpg|thumb|upright|right|Fireplace in the Parlour with plasterwork [[overmantel]] displaying the [[Royal arms of England|royal arms of Queen Elizabeth I]], circa 1559<ref name="Images"/> with [[Caryatid]]s on either side]]
The fortunes of the Moreton family declined during the [[English Civil War]]. As supporters of the [[Cavalier|Royalist]] cause, they found themselves isolated in a community of [[Roundhead|Parliamentarians]].{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=40|ps=none}} Little Moreton Hall was requisitioned by the Parliamentarians in 1643 and used to billet Parliamentary soldiers. The family successfully petitioned for its restitution,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=37–38|ps=none}} and survived the Civil War with their ownership of Little Moreton Hall intact, but financially they were crippled.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=40|ps=none}} They tried to sell the entire estate, but could only dispose of several parcels of land. William Moreton died in 1654 leaving debts of £3,000–£4,000 (equivalent to about £12–16 million as of 2010{{r|MeasuringWorth}}{{efn|Comparing [[Gross domestic product|GDP per capita]] of £3,000 and £4,000 in 1654 with 2010.}}), which forced his heirs to remortgage what remained of the estate.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=38|ps=none}} The family's fortunes never fully recovered, and by the late 1670s they no longer lived in Little Moreton Hall, renting it out instead to a series of tenant farmers. The Dale family took over the tenancy in 1841, and were still in residence more than 100 years later.{{r|Survival}} By 1847 most of the house was unoccupied, and the deconsecrated Chapel was being used as a coal cellar and storeroom.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=42|ps=none}} Little Moreton Hall was in a ruinous condition; its windows were boarded up and its roof was rotten.{{r|RIBA}}

During the 19th century, Little Moreton Hall became "an object of romantic interest" among artists;{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=42|ps=none}} [[Amelia Edwards]] used the house as a setting for her 1880 novel ''Lord Brackenbury''.{{sfnp|Coward|2010|p=329|ps=none}} Elizabeth Moreton, an Anglican nun,{{efn|Elizabeth Moreton (1821–1912) had become a Sister of the [[Community of St John Baptist]] in 1853.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=42|ps=none}}}} inherited the almost derelict house following the death of her sister Annabella in 1892. She restored and refurnished the chapel, and may have been responsible for the insertion of steel rods to stabilise the structure of the Long Gallery. In 1912 she bequeathed the house to a cousin, [[Charles Abraham (bishop of Derby)|Charles Abraham, Bishop of Derby]], stipulating that it must never be sold.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=44|ps=none}}{{efn|The house has never been sold throughout its 500-year history.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=2|ps=none}}}} Abraham opened up Little Moreton Hall to visitors, charging an entrance fee of 6[[Penny (British pre-decimal coin)|d]] (equivalent to about £8 in 2010{{r|MeasuringWorth}}{{efn|Comparing average earnings of 6d in 1912 with 2010.}}) collected by the Dales, who conducted guided tours of the house in return.{{r|Survival}}

Abraham carried on the preservation effort begun by Elizabeth Moreton until he and his son transferred ownership to the National Trust in 1938.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=45|ps=none}} The Dale family continued to farm the estate until 1945, and acted as caretakers for the National Trust until 1955.{{r|Survival}} The Trust has carried out extensive repair and restoration work, including re-roofing; restoration of elements of the hall's original appearance, and removal of some painted patterning added during earlier restoration work.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The familiar black-and-white colour scheme is a fashion introduced by the [[Victorian era|Victorian]]s; originally the oak beams would have been untreated and left to age naturally to a silver colour, and the rendered infill painted [[ochre]].{{sfnp|Lipscomb|2012|loc=loc. Little Moreton Hall|ps=none}} In 1977 it was discovered that the stone slabs on the roof of the south range had become insecure, and work began on a six-phase programme of structural repairs.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=46|ps=none}} Replacement timbers were left in their natural state.{{sfnp|McKenna|1994|p=36|ps=none}}

==House==
[[File:Little Moreton Hall window by Richard de Dale.jpg|thumb|upright|Section of the Withdrawing Room's bay window, showing the patterning of the panes]]
The 100-year construction of Little Moreton Hall coincided with the [[English Renaissance]], but the house is resolutely medieval in design,{{sfnp|Hartwell|Hyde|Hubbard|Pevsner|2011|p=433|ps=none}} apart from some Renaissance decoration such as the [[motif (visual arts)|motifs]] on the Gatehouse,{{sfnp|Fedden|Joekes|1984|p=155|ps=none}} [[Elizabethan architecture|Elizabethan]] fireplaces, and its "extravagant" use of glass.{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|p=90|ps=none}} It is [[timber framing|timber-framed]] throughout except for three brick chimneybreasts and some brick buttressing added at a later date.{{sfnp|Hartwell|Hyde|Hubbard|Pevsner|2011|p=433|ps=none}}

[[Simon Jenkins]] has described Little Moreton Hall as "a feast of medieval carpentry",{{sfnp|Jenkins|2003|p=69|ps=none}} but the building technique is unremarkable for Cheshire houses of the period – an oak framework set on stone [[Foundation (engineering)|footings]]. Diagonal oak braces that create [[Chevron (insignia)|chevron]] and [[Lozenge (shape)|lozenge]] patterns adorn the façades.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=7|ps=none}} The herringbone pattern with [[quatrefoil]]s present at the rear, which can also be seen at [[Haslington Hall|Haslington]] and [[Gawsworth Old Hall|Gawsworth Halls]], is a typical feature of 15th-century work, while the lozenge patterns, continuous middle rail and lack of quatrefoils in the front façade are typical of 16th-century early Elizabethan work.{{sfnp|McKenna|1994|p=13, Fig. 27|ps=none}} The south range containing the gatehouse, the last to be completed, has lighter timbers with a greater variety of patterns.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The timber frame is completed by rendered infill and [[Flemish bond]] brick, or windows.{{r|Pastscape}} The windows contain 30,000 [[Leadlight|leaded panes]] known as quarries, set in patterns of squares, rectangles, lozenges, circles and triangles, complementing the decoration on the timber framing.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=7|ps=none}} Much of the original 16th-century glazing has survived and shows the colour variations typical of old glass.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} Old scratched graffiti is visible in places.{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|p=189|ps=none}}{{efn|One inscription reads: "Man can noe more/know weomen's mind/by kaire/Than by her shadow/hede ye what clothes/Shee weare".}} The older parts of the roof frame are decorated,{{sfnp|McKenna|1994|p=9|ps=none}} and the brickwork of some of the chimneys has [[diapering]] in blue brick.{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|p=185|ps=none}}
[[File:Little Moreton Hall courtyard.jpg|thumbnail|left|The courtyard, facing north toward the Great Hall]]
The house stands on an island surrounded by a 33-foot (10 m) wide moat,{{r|NHLE}}{{efn|The site is marshy, which is at least in part why the oak beams of the house's timber frame stand on sandstone blocks. The moat is kept filled by the high water table.{{sfnp|Fortey|2010|p=21|ps=none}}}} which was probably dug in the 13th or 14th century to enclose an earlier building on the site.{{r|Survival}} There is no evidence that the moat served any defensive purpose, and as with many other moated sites it was probably intended as a status symbol. A sandstone bridge leads to a gatehouse in the three-storey south range,{{r|NHLE}} which has each of its two upper floors [[jettied]] out over the floor beneath.{{r|Goodall}} As is typical of Cheshire's timber-framed buildings the overhanging jetties are hidden by coving,{{sfnp|Pevsner|Hubbard|2003|p=21|ps=none}} which has a recurring quatrefoil decoration.{{sfnp|Hartwell|Hyde|Hubbard|Pevsner|2011|p=435|ps=none}} The Gatehouse leads to a rectangular courtyard, with the Great Hall at the northern end. The two-storey tower to the left of the Gatehouse contains garderobes, which empty directly into the moat.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=21|ps=none}} Architectural historian Lydia Greeves has described the interior of Little Moreton Hall as a "corridor-less warren, with one room leading into another, and four staircases linking different levels".{{sfnp|Greeves|2008|p=201|ps=none}} Some of the grander rooms have fine chimneypieces and wood panelling, but others are "little more than cupboards".{{sfnp|Greeves|2008|p=201|ps=none}} The original purpose of some of the rooms in the house is unknown.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=9|ps=none}}

The Great Hall at the centre of the north range is entered through a porch and screens passage, a feature common in houses of the period, designed to protect the occupants from draughts. As the screens are now missing, they may have been free-standing like those at [[Rufford Old Hall]].{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=10|ps=none}} The porch is decorated with elaborate carvings.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The Great Hall's roof is supported by [[timber roof trusses#Arch-braced truss|arch-braced trusses]],{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=9|ps=none}} which are decorated with carved motifs including dragons.{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|p=186|ps=none}} The floor, now flagged, would probably originally have been rush-covered earth, with a central hearth. The gabled [[bay window]] overlooking the courtyard was added in 1559. The original service wing to the west of the Great Hall, behind the screens passage, was rebuilt in 1546,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=9|ps=none}} and housed a kitchen, [[buttery (room)|buttery]] and pantry.{{r|Goodall}} A hidden shaft was discovered during a 19th-century investigation of two secret rooms above the kitchen, connecting them to a tunnel leading to the moat, the entrance to which has since been filled in.{{sfnp|Smith|2010|p=270|ps=none}} The west range now houses the gift shop and restaurant.

[[File:Little Moreton Hall parlour.jpg|thumbnail|right|A decorated wall in the parlour]]
A doorway behind where the family would have sat at the far end of the hall leads to the Parlour, known as the Little Parlour in surviving 17th-century documents. Together with the adjoining Withdrawing Room and the Great Hall, the Parlour is structurally part of the original building.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=11|ps=none}} The wooden panelling is a [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] addition, behind which the original painted panelling was discovered in 1976.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=13|ps=none}} The decoration consists of painted imitations of marble and inlay,{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} and Biblical scenes, some of which were painted directly onto the plaster and others on paper that was then pasted to the wall. "Crudely drawn" but nevertheless "elaborate", the paintings tell the story of [[Susanna (Book of Daniel)|Susanna and the Elders]] from the [[Biblical apocrypha|Apocrypha]],{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=13|ps=none}} a "favourite Protestant theme".{{sfnp|Greeves|2006|p=226|ps=none}} The Moreton family's wolf head crest and the initials "J.M." suggest a date before John Moreton's death in 1598. Similar painted decoration is found in other Cheshire houses of the late 16th and early 17th centuries.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}}

A private staircase between the Parlour and the Withdrawing Room leads to the first floor. The Withdrawing Room has 16th-century carved wooden panelling, and a wooden ceiling with moulded [[coffer]]ing, which probably dates from 1559 when the Great Hall ceiling was added.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The bay window in this room was also added in 1559, at the same time as the one in the Great Hall. The pair of windows bear the following inscription underneath their gables:
{{Blockquote|God is Al in Al Thing: This windous whire made by William Moreton in the yeare of Oure Lorde MDLIX. Rycharde Dale Carpeder made thies windous by the grac of God.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=29|ps=none}} }}
The wolf head crest also appears in the late 16th-century [[stained glass]] of the Withdrawing Room.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=13|ps=none}} The chimneypiece in this room is decorated with female [[caryatid]]s and bears the arms of Elizabeth I; its plaster would originally have been painted and gilded, and traces of this still remain.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}}

William Moreton III used what is today known as the Exhibition Room as a bedroom in the mid-17th century; it is entered through a doorway from the adjoining Withdrawing Room. Following William's death in 1654 his children Ann, Jane and Philip divided the house into three separate living areas. Ann, whose accommodation was in the Prayer Room above, then used the Exhibition Room as a kitchen. The adjoining Chapel, begun in 1508,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=15|ps=none}} is accessible by a doorway from the courtyard. The Chapel contains Renaissance-style [[tempera]] painting, thought to date from the late 16th century.{{sfnp|Fedden|Joekes|1984|p=156|ps=none}} Subjects include passages from the Bible.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The [[chancel]] was probably a later addition dating from the mid-16th century.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=15|ps=none}} It is separated from the nave by an oak screen and projects eastwards from the main plan of the house, with a much higher ceiling.{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|p=186|ps=none}} The stained glass in the east wall of the chancel is a 20th-century addition installed by Charles Abraham, the last private owner of Little Moreton Hall, as a parting gift on his transfer of ownership to the National Trust.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=17|ps=none}}

The Corn Store adjacent to the Chapel may originally have been used as accommodation for a gatekeeper or steward. By the late 17th century it had been converted into a grain store by raising the floor to protect its contents from damp. Five oak-framed bins inside may have held barley for the Brew-house,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=17|ps=none}} which is now used as a toilet block.

The Guests' Hall and its adjoining Porch Room occupy the space above the entrance to the courtyard and the Gatehouse. They can be accessed either through a doorway from the adjacent Prayer Room or via a staircase at the south end of the courtyard leading to the Long Gallery on the floor above. The first-floor landing leads to a passageway between the Guests' Hall and the Guests' Parlour, and to the garderobe tower visible from the front of the house. A doorway near the entrance to the Guests' Parlour allows access to the Brew-house Chamber, which is above the Brew-house. The Brew-house Chamber was probably built as [[servants' quarters]], and originally accessed via a hatch in the ceiling of the Brew-house below.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=21|ps=none}}

In the mid-17th century the Guests' Hall was referred to as Mr Booth's Chamber, after the genealogist Jack Booth of Tremlowe, a cousin and family friend of the Moreton's and a regular occupant.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=23|ps=none}} Its substantial carved [[corbel|console]]s, inserted not just for decorative effect but to support the weight of the Long Gallery above, have been dated to 1660.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=22|ps=none}} What is today known as the Prayer Room, above the chapel, was originally the chamber of the first William Moreton's daughter Ann, whose maid occupied the adjoining room.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=23|ps=none}}

The floors of the rooms on this level are made from [[Lime-ash floor|lime-ash plaster]] pressed into a bedding of straw and oak laths, which would have offered some protection against the ever-present risk of fire.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=22|ps=none}} All the first-floor rooms in the east range and all except the Prayer Room in the west range are closed to the public, some having been converted into accommodation for the National Trust staff who live on site.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=5|ps=none}}{{r|CheshireLife}} The Education Room in the east range, above what is today the restaurant, was in the mid-16th century a [[solar (room)|solar]], and is now reserved for use by school groups.{{r|VirtualTour}}{{Clear}}

===Upper floor===
Running the entire length of the south range the Long Gallery is roofed with heavy [[gritstone]] slabs,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=6|ps=none}} the weight of which has caused the supporting floors below to bow and buckle.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=44|ps=none}} Architectural historians Peter de Figueiredo and Julian Treuherz describe it as "a gloriously long and crooked space, the wide floorboards rising up and down like waves and the walls leaning outwards at different angles."{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} The crossbeams between the arch-braced roof trusses were probably added in the 17th century to prevent the structure from "bursting apart" under the load.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=18|ps=none}}

[[File:Long Gallery, Little Moreton Hall.jpg|thumb|right|The Long Gallery, looking west]]
The Long Gallery has almost continuous bands of windows along its longer sides to the north and south, and a window to the west; a corresponding window at the east end of the gallery is now blocked.{{sfnp|Hartwell|Hyde|Hubbard|Pevsner|2011|p=434|ps=none}} The end [[tympanum (architecture)|tympana]] have plaster depictions of [[Destiny]] and [[Gad (deity)|Fortune]], copied from [[Robert Recorde]]'s ''Castle of Knowledge'' of 1556.{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}}{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=18–21|ps=none}} The inscriptions read "The wheel of fortune, whose rule is ignorance" and "The speare of destiny, whose rule is knowledge".{{sfnp|Angus-Butterworth|1970|p=187|ps=none}} The Long Gallery was always sparsely furnished, and would have been used for exercising when the weather was inclement and as a games room – four early 17th-century [[real tennis|tennis]] balls have been discovered behind the wood panelling.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=21|ps=none}}

The Upper Porch Room leading off the Long Gallery, perhaps originally intended as a "sanctuary from the fun and games",{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=21|ps=none}} was furnished as a bedroom by the mid-17th century. The fireplace incorporates figures of [[Justice]] and [[Mercy]],{{sfnp|de Figueiredo|Treuherz|1988|pp=119–22|ps=none}} and its central panel contains the Moreton coat of arms quartered with that of the Macclesfield family, celebrating the marriage of John de Moreton to Margaret de Macclesfield in 1329.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=21|ps=none}}{{efn|Margaret de Macclesfield was an heiress to the estate of John de Macclesfield.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=21|ps=none}}}}

===Contents===
Only three pieces of the house's original furniture have survived: a large refectory table, a large cupboard described as a "cubborde of boxes" in an inventory of 1599, possibly used for storing spices, and a "great rounde table" listed in the same inventory.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=10–14|ps=none}}{{sfnp|Bilsborough|1983|pp=133|ps=none}} The refectory table and cupboard are on display in the Great Hall, and the round table in the Parlour, where its octagonal framework suggests that it was designed to sit in the bay window. Except for those pieces, and a collection of 17th-century [[pewter]] tableware in a showcase in the west wall of the Great Hall, the house is displayed with bare rooms.{{sfnp|Greeves|2008|p=201|ps=none}}{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=10–14|ps=none}}

==Gardens and estate==
[[File:Little Moreton Hall garden - geograph.org.uk - 433632.jpg|thumb|left|Replanted knot garden]]
By the mid-16th century the Little Moreton Hall estate was at its greatest extent, occupying an area of {{convert|1360|acre}} and including three [[watermill]]s,{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=28|ps=none}} one of which was used to grind corn. The contours of the pool used to provide power for the cornmill are still visible, although the mill was demolished in the 19th century.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=27|ps=none}} The Moreton family had owned an iron [[bloomery]] in the east of the estate since the late 15th century, and the other two mills were used to drive its [[trip hammer|water-powered hammer]]s. The dam of the artificial pool that provided water for the bloomery's mills, known as Smithy Pool, has survived, although the pool has not. The bloomery was closed in the early 18th century, and the pool and moat were subsequently used for breeding [[carp]] and [[tench]]. By the mid-18th century the estate's main sources of income came from agriculture, timber production, fish farming, and property rentals.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=27|ps=none}}

The earliest reference to a garden at Little Moreton Hall comes from an early 17th-century set of household accounts referring to a gardener and the purchase of some seeds. Philip Moreton, who ran the estate for his older brother Edward in the mid-17th century, left a considerable amount of information on the layout and planting of the area of garden within the moat, to the west of the house. He writes of a herb garden, vegetable garden, and a nursery for maturing fruit trees until they were ready to be transferred to the orchard at the south and east of the house, probably where the orchard is today.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=24–25|ps=none}}

During the 20th century the long-abandoned gardens were replanted in a style sympathetic to the [[Tudor period]]. The [[knot garden]] was planted in 1972, to a design taken from Leonard Meager's ''[[Complete English Gardener]]'', published in 1670.{{sfnp|Fedden|Joekes|1984|pp=155, 257|ps=none}} The intricate design of the knot can be seen from one of the two original viewing mounds, common in 16th-century formal gardening, one inside the moat and the other to the southwest.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|pp=24–25|ps=none}} Other features of the grounds include a [[taxus|yew]] tunnel and an orchard growing fruits that would have been familiar to the house's Tudor occupants: apples, pears, [[quince]]s and [[medlar]]s.{{sfnp|Lake|Hughes|2006|p=27|ps=none}}

==Superstition and haunting==
During the last major restoration work, 18 "assorted boots and shoes" were found hidden in the structure of the building, all dating from the 19th century.{{sfnp|Hoggard|2004|p=180|ps=none}} [[Concealed shoes]] were placed either to ward off demons, ghosts or witches, or to encourage the fertility of the female occupants.{{sfnp|Hoggard|2004|pp=178–79|ps=none}} Like many old buildings, Little Moreton Hall has stories of ghosts; a grey lady is said to haunt the Long Gallery, and a child has reportedly been heard sobbing in and around the chapel.{{r|Jones}}

==Present day==
Little Moreton Hall is open to the public from mid-February to December each year. The ground floor of the west range has been remodelled to include a restaurant and a tearoom whilst a new building houses the visitor reception and shop.{{r|NationalTrust}} Services are held in the Chapel every Sunday from April until October.{{r|Chapel}}{{sfnp|Duckworth|Sankey|2006|p=110|ps=none}}
In common with many other National Trust properties, Little Moreton Hall is available for hire as a film location; in 1996 it was one of the settings for [[ITV Granada|Granada Television]]'s adaptation of [[Daniel Defoe]]'s ''[[Moll Flanders]]'', ''[[The Fortunes and Misfortunes of Moll Flanders (TV series)|The Fortunes and Misfortunes of Moll Flanders]]''.{{r|PeriodDramas}}

3377498.title: Nether Alderley Mill
3377498.extract: Nether Alderley Mill is a 16th-century watermill located in Congleton Road (the A34), to the south of the village of Nether Alderley, Cheshire, England.  It is owned by the National Trust, and is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade II* listed building.  It is a unique example of a triple overshot waterwheel system, two of which are in working order.  It is one of only four virtually complete corn mills in Cheshire.

'''Nether Alderley Mill''' is a 16th-century [[watermill]] located in Congleton Road (the [[A34 road|A34]]), to the south of the village of [[Nether Alderley]], [[Cheshire]], England.  It is owned by the [[National Trust]],<ref name=natt>{{Citation | url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nether-alderley-mill/| title = Nether Alderley Mill| accessdate = 10 March 2012| publisher = [[National Trust]]}}</ref> and is recorded in the [[National Heritage List for England]] as a designated Grade II* [[Listed building#England and Wales|listed building]].<ref name=nhl>{{NHLE |num= 1139592|desc= Nether Alderley Mill and dam wall|accessdate= 10 March 2012|mode=cs2}}</ref>  It is a unique example of a triple [[overshot waterwheel]] system, two of which are in working order.<ref name=napc/>  It is one of only four virtually complete [[Gristmill|corn mills]] in Cheshire.<ref name=natt/>

==History==

The earliest reference to the mill is in 1391.<ref name=nt_bnam>{{Citation |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nether-alderley-mill/features/building-nether-alderley-mill |title=Building Nether Alderley Mill |accessdate=11 August 2022|publisher=[[National Trust]]}}</ref> The 14th-century mill was replaced in 1595–1597, at around the time that ownership of the [[manorialism|manor]] mill passed to the [[Baron Stanley of Alderley|Stanley family]], and some of this late-16th century stonework survives in the mill's basement.<ref name=nt_bnam/><ref name=napc>{{Citation | url = http://www.netheralderleyparish.com/the-local-area/national-trust| title = Nether Alderley Mill| accessdate = 10 March 2012| publisher = Nether Alderley Parish Council}}</ref>

In the mid-18th century, the mill was enlarged to its current size and layout. To provide more power, a new mill pond was built, along with new tunnels, inside which the date 1746 is inscribed.<ref name=nt_bnam/> The new construction appears to have reused much of the stonework and timbers from the 16th-century mill.<ref name=nt_bnam/> Improvements to the mill continued during the 1800s, with a new upper waterwheel and [[cast iron]] mechanism added early in the century, followed by a new lower waterwheel and tailrace tunnels in the 1840s.<ref name=nt_bnam/> Further mechanical improvements included a new cast-iron [[Glossary of mill machinery#Watermill machinery|hurst frame]] and gearing to connect it to the upper waterwheel, installed in the 1870s.<ref name=nt_bnam/>

From the 1880s to 1914 the mill could be operated by a portable 10 [[Horsepower|hp]] [[steam engine]]. The mill closed in about 1939, and the building became derelict.<ref name=napc/> It came into the ownership of the National Trust in 1950.<ref name=past>{{cite PastScape |mnumber=76385|mname=Nether Alderley Mill |accessdate=10 March 2012|mode=cs2}}</ref>  The Trust restored the mill into working order in 1967–70.<ref name=nhl/>

==Architecture and machinery==

The mill is constructed in buff-pink  [[ashlar]] [[sandstone]], and has a long [[shed roof|cat-slide roof]] of [[Kerridge]] stone-slate.  Its plan is rectangular.<ref name=nhl/>  The roof weighs about 200 tons, and is carried in an [[Elizabethan]] oak frame.<ref name=napc/>  The rear wall of the mill forms the dam for the lake supplying the water for the mill; this also acts as a moat for [[Alderley Old Hall]].  The water drives two overshot wheels of {{convert|12|ft|m|1}} and {{convert|13|ft|m|1}} diameter.  Each operates separately, forming in effect two distinct mills with its own machinery, the water passing from the upper wheel to the lower one.<ref name=past/>
