18012152.title: Dunham Massey Hall
18012152.extract:
Dunham Massey Hall, usually known simply as Dunham Massey, is an English country house in the parish of Dunham Massey, in the district of Trafford, Greater Manchester, England. During World War I, it was temporarily used as the Stamford Military Hospital.
It was designated a Grade I listed building on 5 March 1959. It has been owned by the National Trust since the death of Roger Grey, 10th and last Earl of Stamford, in 1976. Dunham Massey was rebuilt in the early 18th century by George Booth, 2nd Earl of Warrington. He had inherited an older mansion from his father, which was in a very poor state of repair.
There were significant alterations, especially internally, at the start of the 20th century. It has historic formal gardens and a deer park. The park and gardens are listed Grade II* on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens.

main.*:
{{Short description|Grade I listed house in Greater Manchester, England}} {{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}} {{Use British English|date=February 2023}} {{Infobox building | image = File:Dunham Massey 2015 105.jpg | alternate_names = Dunham Hall;
Stamford Military Hospital | website = {{URL|http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dunham-massey}} | embedded = {{Designation list |embed = yes |designation1 = Grade I Listed Building |designation1_offname = Dunham Hall |designation1_date = 5 March 1959 |designation1_number = 1356512}} | pushpin_map = Greater Manchester | pushpin_label = Dunham Massey Hall | pushpin_mark = UK Tourist Sign T101 - National Trust property.svg }} '''Dunham Massey Hall''', usually known simply as '''Dunham Massey''', is an [[English country house]] in the parish of [[Dunham Massey]], in the district of [[Trafford]], [[Greater Manchester]], England. During [[World War I]], it was temporarily used as the '''Stamford Military Hospital'''. It was designated a [[Listed buildings in England|Grade I listed building]] on 5 March 1959. It has been owned by the [[National Trust]] since the death of Roger Grey, [[Roger Grey, 10th Earl of Stamford|10th and last Earl of Stamford]], in 1976. Dunham Massey was rebuilt in the early 18th century by [[George Booth, 2nd Earl of Warrington]]. He had inherited an older mansion from his father, which was in a very poor state of repair. There were significant alterations, especially internally, at the start of the 20th century. It has historic [[formal garden]]s and a [[Deer park (England)|deer park]]. The park and gardens are listed Grade II* on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]]. == History == [[Booth Baronets|'Old' Sir George Booth, 1st Baronet]] built the first mansion on the site in the early 17th-century.{{Cite web |title=Booth, Sir George, 2nd Bt. (1622–84), of Dunham Massey, Cheshire. {{!}} History of Parliament Online |url=http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1660-1690/member/booth-sir-george-1622-84 |access-date=12 July 2022 |website=historyofparliamentonline.org}}{{Cite book |last1=Evans |first1=David Morgan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MJylQnvpXQcC&dq=dunham+massey+moat&pg=PA92 |title=The Remains of Distant Times: Archaeology and the National Trust |last2=Salway |first2=Peter |last3=Thackray |first3=David |date=1996 |publisher=Boydell & Brewer |isbn=978-0-85115-671-2 |language=en}}{{Cite book |last=Sambrook |first=Pamela |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=g_UzjpRFaSAC&dq=dunham+massey+moat&pg=PA13 |title=A Country House at Work: Three Centuries of Dunham Massey |date=10 February 2006 |publisher=Pavilion Books |isbn=978-1-905400-19-5 |language=en}} However, the house remained uncompleted by the time of his death and was only completed after the Civil War in the later 17th century by his grandson, [[George Booth, 1st Baron Delamer|'Young' George Booth, 1st Baron Delamer]]. He inherited family debts and spent a considerable amount of energy investing in the future of Dunham Massey Hall; he planted trees to sell for timber and worked to recoup unpaid debts. The [[mansion]]'s service courtyard dates from {{circa|1721}}. The clock tower is inscribed with that date, suggesting that was when improvements were made to the [[stable]]s. In the 1730s, John Norris was brought in to redesign the whole mansion by [[George Booth, 2nd Earl of Warrington|the 2nd Earl of Warrington]], with a design of brick façade accentuated by bays and a stone centrepiece.{{Cite book |last=The National Trust |title=Dunham Massey |year=2000}} [[George Booth, 2nd Earl of Warrington]] died in 1758 and, in a move remarkable for the eighteenth century, ensured that his only child, a daughter, [[Lady Mary Booth]] (1704–72), would inherit and control the estate. She married her cousin, [[Harry Grey, 4th Earl of Stamford]] (1736–68), whose family properties included his estate of [[Enville Hall]]. Lady Mary oversaw the remodelling of the landscape at Dunham Massey, some of which, outside the park wall, was reputedly undertaken by [[Capability Brown|Lancelot Capability Brown]].{{Cite book |last=Stubbs |first=Susie |title=Dunham Massey, Cheshire: a souvenir guide |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-84359-409-3 |location=[England] |pages=4–9, 55 |oclc=823893271}} Their son, [[George Grey, 5th Earl of Stamford|George Harry Grey, 5th Earl of Stamford and Warrington]], inherited both Dunham Massey and Enville Hall, along with other properties. In the 1780s, he commissioned a remodelling of the Great Gallery and the south front of the house by architect [[John Hope (architect)|John Hope]]. He died in 1819 and his son, also [[George Grey, 6th Earl of Stamford|George Harry Grey, but the 6th Earl of Stamford and Warrington]] inherited the estate and began to introduce modernisations to the house. The 6th Earl died in 1845 and his grandson, [[George Grey, 7th Earl of Stamford|George Harry Grey]], inherited it and became the 7th Earl of Stamford. He married twice: first to Elizabeth (Bessie) King Billage, a shoemaker's daughter from Cambridge; the second to Catherine Cocks, a circus performer. However, the local gentry rejected his choices of wife, which led him to leave Dunham Massey and move to Enville Hall. The house was managed by Robert Cox, Catherine's nephew, and rented to tenants for periods in the subsequent fifty years. The descendants of Catherine's niece Sarah Letitia Cox, still occupy [[Enville Hall]] today.{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/cheshire-greater-manchester/dunham-massey/history-of-dunham-massey |title=History of Dunham Massey |publisher=National Trust |access-date=20 April 2025}} The 7th Earl died in 1883 and his cousin, the [[Harry Grey, 8th Earl of Stamford|Reverend Harry Grey]] inherited the title of 8th Earl of Stamford, but never lived at Dunham. At the time of his inheritance, he was living in South Africa, having left England due to alcohol and gambling addictions. He married three times: his first wife Susan Gaydon died in 1869; his second wife Annie Macnamara died in 1874.{{Cite book |last=Squires |first=Anthony E. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=j8B5OAAACAAJ |title=The Greys: A Long and Noble Line: a Biography of the Family of Lady Jane Grey |year=2002 |publisher=Silk Press |isbn=978-1-902685-10-6 |language=en}} His third wife, [[Martha Grey, Countess of Stamford]], a [[Khoekhoe]] woman, was the daughter of a freed, formerly enslaved, woman.{{Cite web |last=africanaunty |date=31 May 2015 |title=The Black Countess {{!}} South Africa Ancestors & Family Tree Research |url=https://www.ancestors.co.za/the-black-countess/ |access-date=12 July 2022 |language=en-GB}} She and the 8th Earl married in 1880. They had two children already, John and Frances, and their third, Mary, was born after they married.{{Cite book |last=Ross |first=R. E. Van der |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KoQnAQAAIAAJ |title=The Black Countess: A Biography |year=2008 |publisher=Ampersand Press |isbn=978-1-919760-75-9 |pages=128 |language=en}} Despite their marriage being recognised by South African law at the time, it was not recognised under English law. This meant that, at the 8th Earl's death in 1890, his son, John, could not inherit and the title passed to [[William Grey, 9th Earl of Stamford]], who was the nephew of the 7th Earl.{{Cite web |title=The Stamford Peerage: Sir George Grey's Cousin Successful |url=https://paperspast.natlib.govt.nz/newspapers/TT18920713.2.27 |access-date=12 July 2022 |website=paperspast.natlib.govt.nz}} He inherited the title, but no assets, until the death of the 7th Countess, Catherine Cox, in 1905. With his wife, Penelope Theobald, they led a programme of restoration for the house. The house was modified in 1905–1908 by architect [[Compton Hall]] and by interior designer [[Percy Macquoid]], in preparation for its reoccupation by William Grey, 9th Earl of Stamford. However, the 9th Earl died in 1910, just as the family was due to move in. Until these modifications, the southern front of the building had 11 three-storey bays; in order to make the building look more 17th-century in style, the third, fourth, eighth and ninth bays were reduced to two storeys, with [[dormer]]s and a centrepiece of three bays was added, with columns each side of the central bay as well as stone [[pediment]]s. William Grey died in 1910 and was succeeded by his son, [[Roger Grey, 10th Earl of Stamford]], who donated the house, its contents, and the {{convert|3,000|acre|adj=on}} estate to the [[National Trust]] at his death in 1976. At the time, it was the trust's most generous bequest in its history. === Stamford Military Hospital === [[File:Dunham Massey 2015 20.jpg|thumb|left|A ward inside Dunham Massey Hall as reconstructed in 2015]] During [[World War I]], Penelope Grey, Countess of Stamford, wife of the 9th Earl of Stamford, made the house available to the [[Red Cross]] as a military hospital, becoming known as the Stamford Military Hospital from April 1917 to January 1919. It hosted 182 injured soldiers who had suffered injuries and needed medical care, but not life-threatening, ranging from gas poisoning to bullets in the brain. The [[hospital]] was run by Sister Catherine Bennett. Lady Stamford's daughter, Lady Jane Grey (later Turnbull), trained as a [[nurse]] at the hospital.{{cite web |date=16 February 2008 |title=Stamford, Earl of (E, 1628–1976) |url=http://www.cracroftspeerage.co.uk/stamford1628.htm |access-date=1 April 2022 |website=Cracroft's Peerage |publisher=Heraldic Media Limited}} From 1 March 2014 until 11 November 2016, the main ward at Stamford Military Hospital (known as "Baghdad"), along with the operating theatre, nurses' station and the recreation room were recreated to commemorate the 100-year anniversary of the start of World War I, along with actors playing the role of characters who worked, lived and recovered at the hospital. == Collections == [[File:Dunham Massey 2015 56.jpg|thumb|The library, with the [[Grinling Gibbons]] carving]] Dunham Massey contains one of the most significant collections of [[Huguenot]] [[silver]], largely collected by [[Booth baronets|George Booth]], [[Earl of Warrington|2nd Earl of Warrington]]. During his 64 years at Dunham Massey, he accumulated over 1000 pieces of silver. One sixth of the original plate remains at Dunham Massey, with much of the collection being dispersed by the Countess of Stamford and Warrington (who died in 1905), widow of George Harry Grey, 7th Earl of Stamford and Warrington (died 1883).{{Cite book |last1=Lomax |first1=James |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yPDjNGzh3isC&q=country+house+silver+from+dunham+massey |title=Country House Silver from Dunham Massey |last2=Rothwell |first2=James |date=30 June 2006 |publisher=Pavilion Books |isbn=978-1-905400-44-7 |pages=127 |language=en}} The [[Earl of Stamford|10th Earl]], [[Roger Grey, 10th Earl of Stamford|Roger Grey]], expended much money and effort in returning family heirlooms originally from Dunham Massey.{{Cite book |title=Dunham Massey |last=The National Trust |year=2000 |pages=29–30}} There is a fine collection of [[oil painting]]s and [[watercolour]]s. The [[relief]] wood-carving of the ''Crucifixion'' by [[Grinling Gibbons]], which hangs in the Library, is the earliest known work by the 17th-century wood carver. It is on this piece that he was working when he was discovered by [[John Evelyn]] in 1671. A group of paintings of the house and estate, known as the ''Harris Views,'' showing the 1730s mansion, were described by [[Simon Jenkins]] as "the most remarkable topographical survey of any country house and its grounds to remain ''in situ''." There is also one painting is from 1690 by Adrien van Diest showing the earlier Elizabethan mansion. Another significant work in the art collection is an ''Allegory of Time'' by [[Guercino]].Jenkins, 80 [[File:Dunham Massey 2016 058.jpg|thumb|The [[Dunham Massey Hall sundial|statue and sundial]] formerly at the front of house]] A [[Dunham Massey Hall sundial|life-sized statue]] of an exoticised black man wearing only a skirt of feathers, in a kneeling position and holding a [[sundial]] above his head, was previously situated at the front of the house. It is believed to have originally been a [[personification]] of [[Africa]], produced by the sculptor [[Andries Carpentière]] in {{circa|1735}} after a figure by [[John van Nost]] for King [[William III of England|William III]]'s privy garden at [[Hampton Court Palace|Hampton Court]].{{citation |title=Sundial |url=http://www.nationaltrustcollections.org.uk/object/936871 |publisher=National Trust |access-date=13 June 2020}} In June 2020, after numerous calls were made for the [[Actions against memorials in Great Britain during the George Floyd protests|removal of statues in Britain with links to the slave trade]] in the wake of the [[murder of George Floyd]], the National Trust said that the decision had been made to move the statue.{{Cite news |date=12 June 2020 |title='Degrading' Dunham Massey Hall statue removed |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-manchester-53011156}}{{Cite web |last=Prior |first=David |date=10 June 2020 |title=Dunham Massey says it is "reviewing" a statue depicting a black figure carrying a sundial |url=http://altrincham.today/2020/06/10/news/dunham-massey-says-reviewing-statue-depicting-black-figure-carrying-sundial/ |access-date=1 April 2022 |website=Altrincham Today}} == Other buildings == [[File:At Dunham Massey 2023 14.jpg|thumb|The carriage house]] The chapel has oak panelling, pews and reredos. The silk wallcoverings in the chapel are a modern recreation, based on the original silk fabric, made in 2015–16.Newman, J., [https://www.humphriesweaving.co.uk/dunham-massey-hall-chapel-silk/ Dunham Massey Hall Chapel Silk], Humphries Weaving, published 23 March 2016, accessed 19 May 2021 The double courtyard house is built of [[Flemish bond]] brick, stone dressings and a roof of Westmorland and Welsh slate. The Carriage House, south of the kitchen courtyard, is Grade I listed. It has a [[Clock tower|clock turret]], which displays a date of 1721. Also south of the hall are the stable buildings, also Grade I listed. They probably date from 1721, but the west side was extended in the 18th century. The Stables Restaurant is located in the upstairs of the South Stables, with an ice-cream parlour below.{{Cite web |title=Eating at Dunham Massey |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/dunham-massey/features/our-cafe-and-restaurant |access-date=8 July 2022 |website=National Trust |language=en}} The oldest surviving building on the Dunham Estate is the watermill, possibly dating back to 1616. Originally built as a corn mill, it was later converted to a saw mill. It is Grade II* listed.{{NHLE|grade=II*|desc=Sawmill|num=1067903|date=5 March 1959}} == Gardens and park == [[File:Dunham Massey Hall 20080803-1.jpg|thumb|Deer in front of the house]] It has historic [[formal garden]]s and a [[Deer park (England)|deer park]]. The park and gardens are listed Grade II* on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].{{NHLE|num=1000853|desc=Dunham Massey|access-date=14 June 2020|mode=cs2|fewer-links=yes}} The park is also a [[List of Sites of Special Scientific Interest in Greater Manchester|Site of Special Scientific Interest]], based on the significance of its mature timber fauna.{{Cite book |last=Bradley |first=Jeremy |url=https://eprints.oxfordarchaeology.com/4360/1/L10996%20Dunham%20Massey%20Final%20Report.pdf |title=The Old Park, Dunham Massey, Trafford, Greater Manchester: Archaeological Investigation and Participation Report |publisher=Oxford Archaeology |year=2017}} The 300 acre [[Deer park (England)|deer park]] at Dunham Massey dates back to [[Middle Ages|medieval times]]. As of 2012, the gardens housed over 700 plant species, as well as 1,600 trees and shrubs; it hosts the largest winter garden in Britain. The Winter Garden has many [[snowdrop]]s, [[daffodil]]s and [[Hyacinthoides non-scripta|bluebells]]. During the [[Second World War]], the eastern part of the estate was requisitioned for use first as a US Army camp and later repurposed as [[Dunham Massey POW Camp]].{{cite web |title=Dunham Massey American Army & German POW Camp |url=http://www.communigate.co.uk/chesh/altrincham/page6.phtml |publisher=Newsquest Media Group Ltd |access-date=28 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101121044430/http://www.communigate.co.uk/chesh/altrincham/page6.phtml |archive-date=21 November 2010}} == Listing and ownership == The stately home was designated a [[Listed buildings in England|Grade I listed building]] on 5 March 1959. It has been owned by the National Trust since the death of the [[Roger Grey, 10th Earl of Stamford|10th and last Earl of Stamford]] in 1976. 557,886 people visited the site in 2025,{{cite web
